claim: Individual cancer cells are generally considered the Darwinian units of selection in malignant populations.
source: Although individual cancer cells are generally considered the Darwinian units of selection in malignant populations, they frequently act as members of groups where fitness of the group cannot be reduced to the average fitness of individual group members.
evidence: This is stated as a general assumption in the field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Cancer cells frequently act as members of groups where fitness of the group cannot be reduced to the average fitness of individual group members.
source: Although individual cancer cells are generally considered the Darwinian units of selection in malignant populations, they frequently act as members of groups where fitness of the group cannot be reduced to the average fitness of individual group members.
evidence: This is a central assertion of the manuscript supported by the examples and framework that follow.

claim: Induction of angiogenesis cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and requires collective actions of groups of cells.
source: For example, induction of angiogenesis, inhibition of the immune system, and niche engineering through environmental acidification and/or remodeling of extracellular matrix cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and require collective actions of groups of cells.
evidence: This is presented as an example of group-level phenomena in cancer, drawing on established biological knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of the immune system cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and requires collective actions of groups of cells.
source: For example, induction of angiogenesis, inhibition of the immune system, and niche engineering through environmental acidification and/or remodeling of extracellular matrix cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and require collective actions of groups of cells.
evidence: This is presented as an example of group-level phenomena in cancer, drawing on established biological knowledge.

claim: Niche engineering through environmental acidification and/or remodeling of extracellular matrix cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and requires collective actions of groups of cells.
source: For example, induction of angiogenesis, inhibition of the immune system, and niche engineering through environmental acidification and/or remodeling of extracellular matrix cannot be achieved by single tumor cells and require collective actions of groups of cells.
evidence: This is presented as an example of group-level phenomena in cancer, drawing on established biological knowledge.

claim: Primary cancers often display high levels of phenotypic and genetic intratumor heterogeneity (ITH).
source: Primary cancers often display high levels of phenotypic and genetic intratumor heterogeneity (ITH).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in cancer biology.

claim: High levels of ITH have been linked to more aggressive tumor behavior.
source: Yet, high levels of ITH have been linked to more aggressive tumor behavior, resistance to therapies, and overall poor prognosis (Marusyk and Polyak, 2010; Meacham and Morrison, 2013; McGranahan and Swanton, 2015; Morris et al., 2016; McGranahan et al., 2017; Dagogo-Jack and Shaw, 2018; Hausser and Alon, 2020; Marusyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: High levels of ITH have been linked to resistance to therapies.
source: Yet, high levels of ITH have been linked to more aggressive tumor behavior, resistance to therapies, and overall poor prognosis (Marusyk and Polyak, 2010; Meacham and Morrison, 2013; McGranahan and Swanton, 2015; Morris et al., 2016; McGranahan et al., 2017; Dagogo-Jack and Shaw, 2018; Hausser and Alon, 2020; Marusyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: High levels of ITH have been linked to overall poor prognosis.
source: Yet, high levels of ITH have been linked to more aggressive tumor behavior, resistance to therapies, and overall poor prognosis (Marusyk and Polyak, 2010; Meacham and Morrison, 2013; McGranahan and Swanton, 2015; Morris et al., 2016; McGranahan et al., 2017; Dagogo-Jack and Shaw, 2018; Hausser and Alon, 2020; Marusyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: ITH can be subdivided into micro-heterogeneity (i.e., cell–cell variability) as well as macro-heterogeneity (i.e., heterogeneous subgroups).
source: ITH can be subdivided into micro-heterogeneity (i.e., cell–cell variability) as well as macro-heterogeneity (i.e., heterogeneous subgroups), yielding a co-existence of either independent genetic subclonal lineages or metastable phenotypic subgroups (Merlo et al., 2006).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Merlo et al., 2006.

claim: Elimination of one subpopulation can induce tumor regression or necrotic collapse.
source: In turn, the co-existence of different subpopulations can profoundly influence global tumor behavior such that elimination of one subpopulation can induce tumor regression or necrotic collapse (Inda et al., 2010; Marusyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Co-existence of different subpopulations can be based on 'cooperation' (or 'mutualism' in ecological terms) between distinct subpopulations.
source: This co-existence can be based on 'cooperation' (or 'mutualism' in ecological terms) between distinct subpopulations (Merlo et al., 2006; Axelrod et al., 2006; Tabassum and Polyak, 2015; Zhou et al., 2017; Martín-Pardillos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Synergistic interactions between two subpopulations of cancer cells may permit metastatic spread.
source: Synergistic interactions between two subpopulations of cancer cells may also permit metastatic spread (Marusyk et al., 2014; Calbo et al., 2011; Neelakantan et al., 2017; Janiszewska et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Reversible phenotype switching seems to have a prominent role in the dynamics of interactions between diverse subclones.
source: Importantly, reversible phenotype switching seems to have a prominent role in the dynamics of interactions between diverse subclones (Chapman et al., 2014), suggesting that the intratumor phenotypic heterogeneity arising from non-genetic variability (i.e., phenotypic plasticity) permits a rapid, reversible strategy for cancer cells to optimally respond to changing environmental conditions and population fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chapman et al., 2014.

claim: Populations of tumor cells exhibit Allee effects in which the proliferation rate paradoxically increases with population size.
source: In addition, populations of tumor cells also exhibit Allee effects (i.e., positive correlation between population density and individual fitness) in which the proliferation rate paradoxically increases with population size, which promotes aggressive tumor growth (see for instance Korolev et al., 2014; Böttger et al., 2015; Sewalt et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Farine et al., 2015 define GPC as 'any descriptor of the types of phenotypes found within a group.'
source: Farine et al., 2015 define GPC as "any descriptor of the types of phenotypes found within a group. Examples include the average body size of individuals, the variation in male color, or the aggressiveness level of the most aggressive individual in the group. In this framework, 'groups' can represent many aspects of the social environments of individuals, including breeding units, social networks, neighborhoods, populations, and communities."
evidence: This is a direct citation of a definition from Farine et al., 2015.

claim: Large groups composed of individuals with similar phenotypes may benefit from a reduced predation pressure because of the confusion effect.
source: For instance, large groups composed of individuals with similar phenotypes may benefit from a reduced predation pressure because of the confusion effect that the lack of prey 'oddity' generates on predators (Landeau and Terborgh, 1986; Krakauer, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Landeau and Terborgh, 1986 and Krakauer, 2004.

claim: In the Daphnia/stickleback system, predation risk is higher on larger individuals.
source: In prey species such as the cladoceran Daphnia magna for which predation risk (by the three-spine stickleback Gasterosteus aculeatus) is higher on larger individuals (i.e., more profitable preys) and confusion effects operate, some conflicts between individuals with different phenotypes might emerge: both large and small individuals benefit from joining groups composed of large individuals, but the presence of small individuals enhances the predation risk experienced by large ones (Rodgers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodgers et al., 2015.

claim: The emergence of macroscopic tumors is dependent on the presence of a threshold number of tumor cells that produce angiogenic factors.
source: For instance, the emergence of macroscopic tumors is dependent on the presence of a threshold number of tumor cells that produce angiogenic factors (Folkman and Klagsbrun, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Folkman and Klagsbrun, 1987.

claim: The enzyme indoleamine-pyrrole 2,3-dioxygenase catalyzes the degradation of tryptophan in the cell's environment leading to the inhibition of cytotoxic immune responses.
source: Another example of a public good is the enzyme indoleamine-pyrrole 2,3-dioxygenase, which catalyzes the degradation of tryptophan in the cell's environment leading to the inhibition of cytotoxic immune responses thereby improving survival of both producing and non-producing cells (Munn and Mellor, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Munn and Mellor, 2016.

claim: Cells that do not produce angiogenic factors can potentially outcompete the producers leading to a collapse of the vascular network.
source: In groups that expand due to sufficiently high proportion of producers, cells that do not produce angiogenic factors (i.e., 'cheaters' that rip the benefits of the common goods without incurring the potential cost associated with their production) can potentially outcompete the producers leading to a collapse of the vascular network (Epstein et al., 2017; Gravenmier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Epstein et al., 2017 and Gravenmier et al., 2018.

claim: CTC clusters have a metastatic potential 23–50 times greater than that of their single-cell counterparts.
source: While these clusters represent a minority of the CTCs found in the bloodstream, they have been shown to have a metastatic potential 23–50 times greater than that of their single-cell counterparts (Aceto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aceto et al., 2014, which provides experimental data.

claim: The presence and size of CTC clusters are associated with worse clinical outcome when compared to single CTCs in multiple cancer types.
source: Moreover, the presence and size of CTC clusters are associated with worse clinical outcome when compared to single CTCs in multiple cancer types (Murlidhar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murlidhar et al., 2017.

claim: CTC clusters can consist of similar or different tumor cells.
source: CTC clusters can consist of similar or different tumor cells (e.g., expressing epithelial or mesenchymal markers).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about CTC cluster composition.

claim: Clusters can include non-tumor cells that can affect the fitness of cancer cells.
source: Clusters can also include non-tumor cells (e.g., blood cells, immune cells, and/or stromal cells) that can affect the fitness of cancer cells (Szczerba et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Szczerba et al., 2019.

claim: Dynamic changes in the epithelial and mesenchymal composition of CTC clusters in breast cancer have been associated with disease progression.
source: For instance, dynamic changes in the epithelial and mesenchymal composition of CTC clusters in breast cancer have been associated with disease progression (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: There are at least nine well-described, independent exceptions of transmissible cancers in the wild.
source: The majority of cancer cells that emerge in multicellular organisms die with their host, but there are at least nine well-described, independent exceptions of transmissible cancers in the wild: one in dogs (called canine transmissible venereal tumor, CTVT), two in Tasmanian devils (called devil facial tumor diseases, DFTD and DFT2), and six in six bivalve species (called bivalve transmissible neoplasias [BTN], see Ujvari et al., 2017; Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ujvari et al., 2017 and Yonemitsu et al., 2019.

claim: Transmissible cancer cells are currently viewed as new parasitic species.
source: These cancer cells are currently viewed as new parasitic species, with their own evolution and dynamics (Dingli and Nowak, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dingli and Nowak, 2006.

claim: Both CTVT and DFTD manifest as undifferentiated cancers, showing strikingly uniform cell morphology.
source: Both CTVT and DFTD manifest as undifferentiated cancers, showing strikingly uniform cell morphology.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about these transmissible cancers.

claim: 105–107 cells were required in transmission experiments for transmissible cancers.
source: Once inside the body of a new host, most transmissible cancer cells fail to establish a new tumor (105–107 cells were required in transmission experiments [House, 1997a; Kreiss et al., 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to House, 1997a and Kreiss et al., 2011, which provide experimental data.

claim: DFT2 avoids immune recognition by various mechanisms including expressing MHC class I molecules that are shared with host devils.
source: For example, the newly emerged devil facial tumor disease, DFT2, avoids immune recognition by various mechanisms: some tumors express MHC class I molecules that are shared with host devils, some express non-classical MHC molecules, while in some﻿ MHC class I, expression has been completely lost (Caldwell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caldwell et al., 2018.

claim: In experimental models of breast cancer heterogeneity, interleukin 11 expressing subpopulations can be responsible for driving tumor growth and metastatic dissemination via mechanisms involving microenvironmental changes.
source: For example, in experimental models of breast cancer heterogeneity, interleukin 11 expressing subpopulations can be responsible for driving tumor growth and metastatic dissemination via mechanisms involving microenvironmental changes (Marusyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marusyk et al., 2014, which provides experimental data.

claim: Aggressive subtypes in glioma and breast cancer can affect, via paracrine signaling, the phenotype and metastatic potential of less aggressive subtypes.
source: Similarly, aggressive subtypes in glioma and breast cancer can affect, via paracrine signaling, the phenotype and metastatic potential of less aggressive subtypes (Neelakantan et al., 2017; Espinoza-Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neelakantan et al., 2017 and Espinoza-Sánchez et al., 2017.

claim: Individual metastatic tumors display marked variability in responses to therapy, ranging from complete elimination to lack of detectable therapeutic responses.
source: Second, in many cases of systemic treatment of multisite metastatic disease, individual tumors display marked variability in responses to therapy, ranging from complete elimination to lack of detectable therapeutic responses (e.g., Patel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2021.

claim: EMT generates mesenchymal-like cells and a variety of intermediate cell states between the epithelial and the mesenchymal state and changes the GPC toward tumor progression and metastasis.
source: EMT generates mesenchymal-like cells and a variety of intermediate cell states between the epithelial and the mesenchymal state and changes the GPC toward tumor progression and metastasis (Brooks et al., 2015; Dongre and Weinberg, 2019; Rios et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2015, Dongre and Weinberg, 2019, and Rios et al., 2019.

claim: Stochasticity of gene expression appears to be increased in cancer cells.
source: Stochasticity of gene expression appears to be increased in cancer cells (Jenkinson et al., 2017), and diverging chromatin states and transcriptional heterogeneity produce corrupted coordination of epigenetic modifications (Pastore et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jenkinson et al., 2017.

claim: The stochastic nature of gene expression fosters a transient resistant phenotype by chance, which can then be stabilized by epigenetic mechanisms.
source: Also, the stochastic nature of gene expression fosters a transient resistant phenotype by chance, which can then be stabilized by epigenetic mechanisms (Shaffer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shaffer et al., 2017.

claim: For genetic predisposition syndromes that confer the highest probability of developing cancer such as those resulting from inherited dysfunction of BRCA1/2 and mismatch repair genes, a significant proportion of patients (30–40%) do not develop cancer by the age of 70.
source: It is noteworthy that even for genetic predisposition syndromes that confer the highest probability of developing cancer such as those resulting from inherited dysfunction of BRCA1/2 (predisposing to breast and ovarian cancers) and mismatch repair genes (e.g., Lynch syndrome), a significant proportion of patients (30–40%) do not develop cancer by the age of 70 (Antoniou and Easton, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Antoniou and Easton, 2006, which provides clinical data.

claim: Tumors have been described as composed of functional compartments with a division of labor among these compartments.
source: Tumors have already been described as composed of functional compartments with a division of labor among these compartments (Grunewald et al., 2011; Hausser et al., 2019) and conceived as a whole consortium of cooperating malignant clones (Ramón Y Cajal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grunewald et al., 2011, Hausser et al., 2019, and Ramón Y Cajal et al., 2017.

claim: Tumors have been conceived as a whole consortium of cooperating malignant clones.
source: Tumors have already been described as composed of functional compartments with a division of labor among these compartments (Grunewald et al., 2011; Hausser et al., 2019) and conceived as a whole consortium of cooperating malignant clones (Ramón Y Cajal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ramón Y Cajal et al., 2017.

claim: The mutational and epigenetic mechanisms that generate heterogeneity in cancers are relatively well understood.
source: Whereas the mutational and epigenetic mechanisms that generate this heterogeneity are relatively well understood, mechanisms responsible for maintaining this heterogeneity in cancer cell populations, as well as the impact of ITH on clinically important properties of the disease, are less clear.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mechanisms responsible for maintaining heterogeneity in cancer cell populations are less clear.
source: Whereas the mutational and epigenetic mechanisms that generate this heterogeneity are relatively well understood, mechanisms responsible for maintaining this heterogeneity in cancer cell populations, as well as the impact of ITH on clinically important properties of the disease, are less clear.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The impact of ITH on clinically important properties of the disease is less clear.
source: Whereas the mutational and epigenetic mechanisms that generate this heterogeneity are relatively well understood, mechanisms responsible for maintaining this heterogeneity in cancer cell populations, as well as the impact of ITH on clinically important properties of the disease, are less clear.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A deeper understanding of ITH at different stages during cancer progression might result in novel therapeutic strategies directed at altering tumor composition towards decreased malignancy.
source: Thus, a deeper understanding of ITH at different stages during cancer progression might result in novel therapeutic strategies directed at altering tumor composition towards decreased malignancy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future therapeutic applications.

claim: Stable co-existence of distinct subpopulations or subclones within tumor cell populations that follow Darwinian dynamics appears to be counterintuitive.
source: In particular, stable co-existence of distinct subpopulations or subclones within tumor cell populations that follow Darwinian dynamics appears to be counterintuitive.
evidence: This is a theoretical observation about the apparent paradox of stable heterogeneity.

claim: The maintenance of stable subpopulations with heritable phenotypes within the same tumor indicates the presence of multiple niches producing complex patterns of co-existence.
source: Indeed, the maintenance of stable subpopulations with heritable phenotypes within the same tumor indicates the presence of multiple niches producing complex patterns of co-existence, although weak stabilizing selection and drift may also contribute to phenotypic variability.
evidence: This is an inference about what stable heterogeneity implies about tumor ecology.

claim: Tumor growth and progression are associated with changes in microenvironmental contexts in space and time.
source: Tumor growth and progression are associated with changes in microenvironmental contexts in space and time (such as acidification, inflammatory response, hypoxia etc.).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in cancer biology.

claim: A GPC that is highly 'optimal' during the early stages of tumorigenesis may not be optimal in a large tumor.
source: Thus, a GPC that is highly 'optimal' (reflected in proliferation and death of subgroup members, as well as in expansion of the group) during the early stages of tumorigenesis (e.g., composed of highly proliferative cells) may not be optimal in a large tumor (which requires vasculature) (Losi et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2018; Figure 2; steps 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The transition to a metastatic tumor relies on a different 'optimal' GPC that reflects changes in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Similarly, the transition to a metastatic tumor relies on a different 'optimal' GPC (e.g., including a higher proportion of 'aggressive' cells) that reflects changes in the tumor microenvironment (Figure 2; step 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: Differences in the overall context prior to cancer initiation, such as genetic makeup, sex, hormonal environment, aging, are expected to alter the match between GPC and its impact on the fitness of the group.
source: In addition to these spatio-temporal contextual changes within dynamic tumors, the differences in the overall context prior to cancer initiation, such as genetic makeup, sex, hormonal environment, aging, are expected to alter the match between GPC and its impact on the fitness of the group (Laconi et al., 2020; Vibishan and Watve, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Laconi et al., 2020 and Vibishan and Watve, 2020.

claim: Successful metastatic colonization is achieved by clusters of CTCs rather than by individual tumor cells in many cases.
source: In many cases, successful metastatic colonization is achieved by clusters of CTCs rather than by individual tumor cells (Heeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heeke et al., 2019.

claim: Most cancers are not transmissible and hence cannot evolve for longer periods than the life expectancy of their host.
source: Noticeable ecological and evolutionary singularities however exist, given that most cancers are not transmissible and hence cannot evolve for longer periods than the life expectancy of their host, and because tumors are usually not in competition inside the hosts (except in transmissible tumors like DFTD and DFT2 in Tasmanian devils, see Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of most cancers, with a citation to Thomas et al., 2018 for the exception.

claim: Tumors are usually not in competition inside the hosts except in transmissible tumors like DFTD and DFT2 in Tasmanian devils.
source: Noticeable ecological and evolutionary singularities however exist, given that most cancers are not transmissible and hence cannot evolve for longer periods than the life expectancy of their host, and because tumors are usually not in competition inside the hosts (except in transmissible tumors like DFTD and DFT2 in Tasmanian devils, see Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2018.

claim: To become transmissible, a cancer must gain the ability to shed a very large number of cells that can both survive in the environment outside the host's body and be able to infect new hosts.
source: However, to become transmissible, a cancer must also gain the ability to shed a very large number of cells that can both survive in the environment outside the host's body (Sunila and Farley, 1989), but also be able to infect new hosts (Ujvari et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sunila and Farley, 1989 and Ujvari et al., 2016b.

claim: Variability in antigen expression in and between CTVT and DFTD tumors has been observed.
source: However, the tumors are not completely homogeneous, and variability in antigen expression in and between tumors has been observed (O'Neill, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Neill, 2011.

claim: CTVT and DFTD cancer lineages have continued to evolve since their initial emergence.
source: In contrast, in transmissible cancers, clonal cell lineages are passed from host to host, and thus evolve as novel parasitic life forms, as seen in CTVT and DFTD, where these cancer lineages have continued to evolve since their initial emergence (Pearse et al., 2012; Dujon et al., 2020a; Kwon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pearse et al., 2012, Dujon et al., 2020a, and Kwon et al., 2020.

claim: The major focus of therapeutic development is on directly targeting viability or proliferation of tumor cells.
source: Currently, the major focus of therapeutic development is on directly targeting viability or proliferation of tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about current therapeutic approaches.

claim: Targeting keystone tumor cell subgroups will be more efficient than targeting the entire heterogeneous tumor because it would target smaller and more homogenous and less diverse subgroups.
source: This strategy, compared to those that target the entire heterogeneous tumor, will be more efficient because it would target smaller and more homogenous and less diverse subgroups.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: Targeting smaller and more homogenous subgroups should decrease the risk of emergence of resistant clones.
source: This should decrease the risk of emergence of resistant clones.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic outcomes.

claim: Recent advances in single-cell analyses are providing detailed characterization of phenotypes of individual tumor cells and/or subgroups that constitute the GPC.
source: Recent advances in single-cell analyses, such as single-cell RNA sequencing and high multiplexing histological analyses, are already providing us with detailed characterization of phenotypes of individual tumor cells and/or subgroups that constitute the GPC.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about current technological capabilities.

claim: Targeting phenotypic plasticity might be able to prevent plastic adaptive changes in GPC and improve therapeutic outcomes.
source: Therefore, explicitly targeting phenotypic plasticity (independently of cytotoxic/cytostatic effects of treatment) might be able to prevent plastic adaptive changes in GPC and improve therapeutic outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: Targeting molecular machinery involved in phenotypic rewiring should limit the evolution of the GPC both during tumor growth and after a therapeutic intervention.
source: Thus, targeting molecular machinery involved in phenotypic rewiring (such as inhibitors of HDAC, KDM, BETs) should limit the evolution of the GPC both during tumor growth and after a therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: Enhanced cellular stochasticity in cancer cells would facilitate phenotypic conversions toward novel states.
source: The enhanced cellular stochasticity in cancer cells would facilitate these phenotypic conversions toward novel states (Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: Modulating stochasticity, especially through tuning of gene expression variability, might represent a good strategy to control tumoral GPC evolution.
source: As such, modulating stochasticity, especially through tuning of gene expression variability, might represent a good strategy to control tumoral GPC evolution (reduced phenotypic heterogeneity will limit cooperative interactions).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: Global epigenetic changes generally observed in cancer cell epigenomes could find their origin in 'tumor reprogramming' due to genetic alterations initiating cancer.
source: The global epigenetic changes generally observed in cancer cell epigenomes could find their origin in 'tumor reprogramming' due to genetic alterations initiating cancer that would contribute to cancer growth less by inducing cell proliferation than by causing 'developmental reprogramming' of the epigenome and allowing cells to aberrantly and pathologically differentiate (Vicente-Dueñas et al., 2015; Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vicente-Dueñas et al., 2015 and Xiong et al., 2019.

claim: Global destabilization of gene expression could originate from tissue disruption-induced stochasticity.
source: Another possibility is that this global destabilization of gene expression could originate from tissue disruption-induced stochasticity (Capp, 2005; Capp, 2017; Capp, 2019; Capp and Bataille, 2020), suggesting that restoring cellular interactions present in the initial tissue for instance with molecules that would mimic healthy cellular interactions would reduce cell stochasticity and restabilize cellular phenotypes (Capp and Bataille, 2020; Capp, 2012; Capp and Bataille, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Capp and colleagues' work.

claim: If the optimum GPC needs to be reestablished at a metastatic site, the failure to do so could contribute to the extremely low colonization rate of circulating tumor cells.
source: Consequently, if the optimum GPC needs to be reestablished at a metastatic site, the failure to do so could contribute (along with the many other hurdles faced by prospective metastases) to the extremely low colonization rate of circulating tumor cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about factors affecting metastatic colonization.

claim: Disrupting clonal cooperation by targeting key factors was already suggested.
source: For instance, disrupting clonal cooperation by targeting key factors was already suggested (Zhou et al., 2017), as well as their shared external products (i.e., 'public goods') (Pepper, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2017 and Pepper, 2012.

claim: Inhibition of tumor progression can be achieved by disruption of clonal cooperative interactions.
source: Inhibition of tumor progression can be achieved by disruption of these clonal cooperative interactions, which impair the tumor ecosystem and the tumoral GPC.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic outcomes.

claim: The GPC concept permits assessment of some of the functional aspects of cancer dynamics, which are impossible to understand by simply examining cellular collections only.
source: A first obvious benefit of the GPC concept resides in the fact that it permits assessment of some of the functional aspects of cancer dynamics, which are impossible to understand by simply examining cellular collections only.
evidence: This is an assertion about the utility of the GPC framework.

claim: The utility of considering tumor GPC is currently limited by the lack of criteria to define relevant groups of tumor cells.
source: On the other hand, the utility of considering tumor GPC is currently limited by the lack of criteria to define relevant groups of tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation of the GPC framework.

claim: The formation of 'the right GPC' is heavily influenced by chance, stochasticity and spatial context.
source: Still, the formation of 'the right GPC', appearing in the right condition at the right time, is heavily influenced by chance, stochasticity and spatial context, and thus remains challenging to investigate and act on.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of GPC formation.

claim: The propensity for developing the 'right' GPC during tumorigenesis may rely on the individual's genetic predisposition.
source: Other information is also needed to determine whether the propensity for developing the 'right' GPC (see Figure 2) during tumorigenesis may rely on the individual's genetic predisposition.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about factors affecting GPC formation.

claim: The GPC might be an important modulating factor of cancer risk over time.
source: The GPC might well be an important modulating factor of the risk over time.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the role of GPC in cancer risk.

claim: Figure 1 shows that individuals show significant phenotypic variation.
source: Because individuals show significant phenotypic variation (I), groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group (II). This may in return influence group-level outcomes (III), which as a consequence differentially impacts individual fitness (IV). (V) GPC then drives different evolutionary responses, like for instance decisions to join or leave particular groups or phenotypic plasticity in response to GPC. These phenomena can then influence the distribution of phenotypes in subsequent generations (figure modified from Farine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, which illustrates the GPC framework.

claim: Groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group.
source: Because individuals show significant phenotypic variation (I), groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group (II). This may in return influence group-level outcomes (III), which as a consequence differentially impacts individual fitness (IV). (V) GPC then drives different evolutionary responses, like for instance decisions to join or leave particular groups or phenotypic plasticity in response to GPC. These phenomena can then influence the distribution of phenotypes in subsequent generations (figure modified from Farine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, which illustrates the GPC framework.

claim: GPC may influence group-level outcomes.
source: Because individuals show significant phenotypic variation (I), groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group (II). This may in return influence group-level outcomes (III), which as a consequence differentially impacts individual fitness (IV). (V) GPC then drives different evolutionary responses, like for instance decisions to join or leave particular groups or phenotypic plasticity in response to GPC. These phenomena can then influence the distribution of phenotypes in subsequent generations (figure modified from Farine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, which illustrates the GPC framework.

claim: Group-level outcomes differentially impact individual fitness.
source: Because individuals show significant phenotypic variation (I), groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group (II). This may in return influence group-level outcomes (III), which as a consequence differentially impacts individual fitness (IV). (V) GPC then drives different evolutionary responses, like for instance decisions to join or leave particular groups or phenotypic plasticity in response to GPC. These phenomena can then influence the distribution of phenotypes in subsequent generations (figure modified from Farine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, which illustrates the GPC framework.

claim: GPC drives different evolutionary responses, like decisions to join or leave particular groups or phenotypic plasticity in response to GPC.
source: Because individuals show significant phenotypic variation (I), groups may vary in their GPC depending on which individuals constitute the group (II).
